49-nord-6-est-frac-lorraine.name: Fonds régional d'art contemporain de Lorraine
49-nord-6-est-frac-lorraine.description: Regional collection of contemporary art founded in 1983, housed since 2004 in the Hôtel Saint-Livier, the oldest private mansion in Metz, parts of which date back to the 12th century. Its collection brings together more than nine hundred works by around three hundred artists, including numerous immaterial pieces.

abbaye-de-beaulieu-en-rouergue.name: Beaulieu-en-Rouergue Abbey
abbaye-de-beaulieu-en-rouergue.description: Cistercian abbey founded in 1144 by monks from Clairvaux in the Seye valley, in the Rouergue. Sold as national property in 1791 and given to the state in 1973, it preserves its Gothic church and chapter house and now houses one of the finest collections of postwar French art (1945-1975).

abbaye-de-charroux.name: Charroux Abbey
abbaye-de-charroux.description: Benedictine abbey founded in 785 by Count Roger of Limoges under the protection of Charlemagne, famed for its relic of the Holy Prepuce and for a rotunda plan unique in France. All that survives is the octagonal lantern tower known as the Tour Charlemagne, 37 metres high, along with fragments of the cloister and chapter house.

abbaye-de-cluny.name: Cluny Abbey
abbaye-de-cluny.description: Benedictine abbey founded in 910 by Duke William I of Aquitaine, cradle of the Cluniac order, which grew to include some one thousand monasteries across Europe. Its Cluny III abbey church, begun in 1088, was the largest church in Christendom until St Peter's in Rome was rebuilt; sold as national property and largely demolished after 1798, only the Eau Bénite bell tower and south transept survive.

abbaye-de-graville.name: Graville Abbey
abbaye-de-graville.description: Former priory of Augustinian canons founded in 1203 by Guillaume Malet, whose Romanesque and Gothic church, dedicated to Saint Honorine, overlooks the Seine estuary. Restored from 1840 onward, the abbey houses a museum rich in medieval sculpture and religious statuary, as well as a collection of house models.

abbaye-de-la-sauve-majeure.name: La Sauve-Majeure Abbey
abbaye-de-la-sauve-majeure.description: Benedictine abbey founded in 1079 by Gérard de Corbie, a major waypoint on the pilgrim routes to Santiago de Compostela and listed for that role as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1998. Ruined since the 19th century, it preserves its Romanesque chevet and more than eighty carved capitals, one of the richest ensembles of Romanesque sculpture in the Gironde.

abbaye-de-montmajour.name: Montmajour Abbey
abbaye-de-montmajour.description: Benedictine abbey founded in 948 near Arles, which grew into one of the wealthiest in Provence, as its Notre-Dame abbey church (1130-1182), Romanesque cloister, Sainte-Croix chapel and troglodyte Saint-Pierre hermitage still attest. Abandoned after the Revolution, it inspired numerous drawings by Van Gogh in 1888.

abbaye-de-vaucelles.name: Vaucelles Abbey
abbaye-de-vaucelles.description: Cistercian abbey founded in 1132 as a daughter house of Clairvaux, in the Escaut valley; its abbey church ranked among the largest Cistercian churches in Europe before being dismantled after the Revolution. What survives is the monks' building from the late 12th century and its chapter house with Gothic vaulting.

abbaye-des-premontres.name: Abbaye des Prémontrés
abbaye-des-premontres.description: Former abbey of Premonstratensian canons rebuilt between 1705 and 1735 under Duke Leopold I, to the plans of the architect-monks Thomas Mordillac and Nicolas Pierson. Bombed in 1944 and later restored, it became a cultural centre in 1964, renowned for its hall-church and its oval staircase known as the Atlante.

abbaye-du-bec-hellouin.name: Bec Abbey
abbaye-du-bec-hellouin.description: Benedictine abbey founded in 1034 by Herluin, whose school, led first by Lanfranc and then by Anselm, both future archbishops of Canterbury, became renowned across medieval Europe. Turned into a military horse depot under Napoleon, it regained a monastic community in 1948; visitors can see the 15th-century Saint-Nicolas tower and the cloister.

abbaye-du-mont-saint-michel.name: Mont-Saint-Michel Abbey
abbaye-du-mont-saint-michel.description: Sanctuary founded around 708 by Bishop Aubert of Avranches, which became a Benedictine abbey in 966, built atop a rocky islet exposed to the bay's powerful tides. The Merveille, a Gothic ensemble of stacked halls built between 1211 and 1228, was added to the 11th-century Romanesque church; a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1979, the abbey has hosted the Monastic Fraternities of Jerusalem since 2001.

abbaye-du-thoronet.name: Thoronet Abbey
abbaye-du-thoronet.description: Cistercian abbey founded in 1146, the oldest of the 'three Provençal sisters' alongside Sénanque and Silvacane, built of local stone between 1160 and 1180. UNESCO regards it as the most accomplished example of Cistercian architecture; restored between 1985 and 1990, it now serves as a museum and concert venue.

abri-pataud.name: Abri Pataud
abri-pataud.description: Rock shelter on the banks of the Vézère, occupied by Upper Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers between roughly 35,000 and 20,000 years before present. Excavated from 1958 to 1964 by the American archaeologist Hallam L. Movius, it is managed by the National Museum of Natural History and displays its stratigraphy in situ.

alignements-de-carnac.name: Carnac Stones
alignements-de-carnac.description: Nearly 3,000 standing stones erected around 2500 BC over some 4 kilometres, arranged in three main alignments — Ménec, Kermario and Kerlescan. Their purpose remains uncertain and has prompted many theories; the site joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2025.

amphoralis.name: Amphoralis
amphoralis.description: Site museum devoted to a vast Gallo-Roman pottery workshop active from the 1st to the 3rd century, excavated from 1976 under the direction of Fanette Laubenheimer. Opened in 1992, it displays the remains of the kilns and the potters' dwellings, who mainly produced Gauloise 4-type wine amphorae.

apothicairerie-de-l-hotel-dieu-le-comte.name: Apothecary of the Hôtel-Dieu-le-Comte
apothicairerie-de-l-hotel-dieu-le-comte.description: Pharmacy of the former Hôtel-Dieu-le-Comte, a hospital founded in the 12th century by Count Henry I of Champagne, preserved in its 18th-century decor. It brings together hundreds of faience jars, painted wooden boxes known as silènes, and pewter and glass flasks, along with the great laboratory.

appartement-temoin-perret.name: Perret Show Apartment
appartement-temoin-perret.description: Furnished apartment recreated in a building from the reconstruction led by Auguste Perret after the destruction of Le Havre in 1944. It recreates the comforts and furnishings of the 1950s, at the heart of a city centre listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.

arc-de-triomphe.name: Arc de Triomphe
arc-de-triomphe.description: Triumphal arch commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 and completed in 1836 at the top of the Champs-Élysées. It shelters the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, and its rooftop terrace overlooks the twelve avenues radiating from Place de l'Étoile.

archea-archeologie-en-pays-de-france.name: ARCHÉA, Archaeology in Pays de France
archea-archeologie-en-pays-de-france.description: Archaeology museum of the Roissy Pays de France area, opened in Louvres in 2010. Its displays come from local excavations, notably the medieval castle of Orville and the potters' workshops of Fosses, spanning two millennia of life north of Paris.

arenes-de-lutece.name: Arènes de Lutèce
arenes-de-lutece.description: Remains of a 1st-century Gallo-Roman amphitheatre in the Latin Quarter, which could seat around 15,000 spectators for plays and combat games. Rediscovered in 1869 during building works, the arena now serves as a public square.

arsenal-saint-jean-musee-d-art-contempor.name: Arsenal Saint-Jean – Museum of Contemporary Art
arsenal-saint-jean-musee-d-art-contempor.description: Housed since 1995 in a 19th-century arsenal south of the town centre, this museum presents the contemporary art collection of the city of Soissons, one of the leading such collections in Hauts-de-France with some four hundred inventoried works. It also hosts regular temporary exhibitions.

artotheque-d-angers-repaire-urbain.name: Artothèque d'Angers — Repaire Urbain
artotheque-d-angers-repaire-urbain.description: Art-lending library of the Angers museums, housed at the Repaire Urbain, boulevard du Roi-René. It holds a collection of contemporary artworks that the public can borrow, and puts them on display through changing hangs in its spaces.

artotheque-d-angouleme.name: Artothèque d'Angoulême
artotheque-d-angouleme.description: Municipal art-lending library attached to the Angoulême Museum, housed on rue de Bordeaux on the site of the former Paper Museum. It offers the loan of contemporary artworks from its collection, as well as hangs open to the public.

basilique-cathedrale-de-saint-denis.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis
basilique-cathedrale-de-saint-denis.description: Abbey church rebuilt from 1135 under Abbot Suger and regarded as the birthplace of Gothic architecture. Necropolis of the French monarchy, it holds more than seventy recumbent effigies and tombs, from Dagobert to Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette.

basilique-du-sacre-coeur-de-montmartre.name: Sacré-Cœur Basilica
basilique-du-sacre-coeur-de-montmartre.description: Romano-Byzantine basilica crowning the Montmartre hill, begun in 1875 as a national vow and consecrated in 1919. Its white domes are a Paris landmark, and the esplanade in front offers a sweeping panorama over the city.

beffroi-de-dreux-ancien-hotel-de-ville-r.name: Dreux Belfry
beffroi-de-dreux-ancien-hotel-de-ville-r.description: Former town hall of Dreux, built from 1512 to 1537 by Pierre Chéron, Jean des Moulins and then Clément Métezeau in the Louis XII style, at the hinge between Flamboyant Gothic and the early Renaissance. Listed as a historic monument as early as 1840, it is the only monument of its kind in Eure-et-Loir.

bibliotheque-humaniste-de-selestat.name: Sélestat Humanist Library
bibliotheque-humaniste-de-selestat.description: Library formed from the union of the collection of Sélestat's Latin school, founded in 1452, and the personal library of the humanist Beatus Rhenanus, bequeathed to the town in 1547 and inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. The collections are displayed in the former grain hall, redesigned by Rudy Ricciotti and reopened in 2018.

bourse-de-commerce-pinault-collection.name: Bourse de Commerce – Pinault Collection
bourse-de-commerce-pinault-collection.description: Contemporary art museum opened in 2021 in the former Paris commodities exchange, a circular building crowned by a 19th-century glass-and-iron dome. Redesigned by Tadao Ando, it presents rotating exhibitions from François Pinault's collection.

cabinet-des-monnaies-et-medailles.name: Marseille Coin and Medal Cabinet
cabinet-des-monnaies-et-medailles.description: Numismatic cabinet of the Marseille museums, housed on rue Clovis-Hugues within the municipal archives. It holds nearly 50,000 coins, medals and objects, including the Auriol hoard discovered in 1867 and some 8,000 medals from the 15th to the 20th century.

cairn-centre-d-art-contemporain.name: CAIRN Centre for Contemporary Art
cairn-centre-d-art-contemporain.description: Contemporary art centre of national interest created in 2000, the first venue of its kind in Alpes-de-Haute-Provence. Built around artist residencies engaging with the region's mineral landscapes, it forms the Ambulo hub together with the Gassendi Museum and the Alexandra David-Néel House.

cairn-de-barnenez.name: Barnenez Cairn
cairn-de-barnenez.description: Neolithic cairn built around 4700 BC, one of the oldest monuments in Europe, 75 metres long and containing eleven passage graves built in two phases. Threatened by a quarry in 1955, it was saved through the intervention of archaeologist Pierre-Roland Giot.

capc-musee-d-art-contemporain-de-bordeau.name: CAPC Museum of Contemporary Art, Bordeaux
capc-musee-d-art-contemporain-de-bordeau.description: Museum housed in the Entrepôt Lainé, a vast brick warehouse built in 1824 for the colonial goods trade. Founded in 1973 as a centre for contemporary visual arts and elevated to museum status in 1984, it holds a collection of art from the 1960s to the present and stages its exhibitions in the nave.

carmel-maison-de-patrimoine.name: Le Carmel — Heritage House
carmel-maison-de-patrimoine.description: Former Capuchin convent taken over in 1821 by the Carmelites of Abbeville, who occupied it until 1998. Acquired by the town in 2011 and protected as a historic monument in 2021, it preserves its 17th- and 19th-century conventual buildings, its gardens, and the largest collection of sacred art in the Somme.

carre-d-art-musee-d-art-contemporain.name: Carré d'Art
carre-d-art-musee-d-art-contemporain.description: Glass-and-steel building designed by Norman Foster and inaugurated in 1993 opposite the Maison Carrée, whose proportions it echoes. It houses the municipal media library and a museum of contemporary art whose collection, comprising several hundred works since 1960, focuses on the French, Mediterranean and Anglo-Saxon art scenes.

cathedrale-de-besancon-et-son-horloge-as.name: Besançon Cathedral and Astronomical Clock
cathedrale-de-besancon-et-son-horloge-as.description: Besançon's Saint-Jean Cathedral, whose astronomical clock was built between 1857 and 1860 by clockmaker Auguste-Lucien Vérité. Its roughly 30,000 parts drive 122 dials and automatons displaying hours, tides, eclipses and religious feast days from around the world.

cathedrale-et-tresor-de-chartres.name: Chartres Cathedral and Treasury
cathedrale-et-tresor-de-chartres.description: Gothic cathedral built largely within the thirty years following the fire of 1194 and consecrated in 1260, famed for its 13th-century stained-glass windows and their inimitable blue. Its treasury, reopened in 2024, holds the Veil of the Virgin (Sancta Camisia), venerated since the 9th century.

cathedrale-notre-dame-de-paris.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
cathedrale-notre-dame-de-paris.description: Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, built between 1163 and 1345, famed for its twin-towered façade, rose windows and flying buttresses. Damaged by fire in 2019, it reopened to visitors in December 2024 after restoration.

centre-d-art-de-la-photographie-espace-r.name: Centre for Photography — Espace Romain-Rolland
centre-d-art-de-la-photographie-espace-r.description: Art centre devoted to contemporary photography, opened in 2025 in a former primary school in Bergerac's historic centre. It has 240 square metres of exhibition space, an artist studio-residency and an education room, and refreshes its exhibitions throughout the year.

centre-d-histoire-de-la-resistance-et-de.name: Centre for the History of Resistance and Deportation
centre-d-histoire-de-la-resistance-et-de.description: Museum opened in 1992 in Lyon's former military health school, a building occupied by Klaus Barbie's Gestapo from 1943 to 1944. Its permanent exhibition traces the Occupation, the Resistance and deportation in the Lyon region through archives, objects and filmed testimony.

centre-de-la-resistance-de-la-deportatio.name: Centre of the Resistance, Deportation and Memory
centre-de-la-resistance-de-la-deportatio.description: Memorial centre for the Second World War, housed since September 2019 on place Victor-Hugo, near the royal château. Across 225 square metres, its permanent exhibition brings together period archives and objects — weapons, uniforms, photographs — partly bequeathed by former Resistance members and deportees, complemented by temporary exhibitions.

centre-de-la-vieille-charite-cvc.name: Vieille Charité Centre (CVC)
centre-de-la-vieille-charite-cvc.description: Former almshouse for the poor, built from 1671 to 1749 in the heart of the Panier district to designs by Pierre Puget, around a chapel with an oval dome. Restored from the 1970s onward, it now houses the Museum of Mediterranean Archaeology and the Museum of African, Oceanian and Native American Arts.

centre-jeanne-d-arc.name: Joan of Arc Centre
centre-jeanne-d-arc.description: Centre for study and documentation created in 1974 by the historian Régine Pernoud with the support of André Malraux, today a department of the city of Orléans. It brings together some 22,000 printed works, 41 manuscripts from the 15th to 18th centuries, more than 4,600 photographic documents and around fifty films devoted to Joan of Arc.

chapelle-des-cordeliers-vitrail-de-marc-.name: Cordeliers Chapel (Marc Chagall Stained-Glass Window)
chapelle-des-cordeliers-vitrail-de-marc-.description: Former chapel of Sarrebourg's Franciscan convent, medieval in origin, deconsecrated during the Revolution and later restored to house contemporary art. Its great west window has been filled since 1976 by a monumental stained-glass window by Marc Chagall entitled La Paix (Peace), some twelve metres high.

chapelle-des-moines-de-berze-la-ville.name: Monks' Chapel of Berzé-la-Ville
chapelle-des-moines-de-berze-la-ville.description: Romanesque chapel of the priory given in 1100 to Hugh of Semur, abbot of Cluny, as a retreat residence. Its early-12th-century murals, rediscovered in 1887 beneath whitewash, rank among the finest surviving examples of Cluniac art.

chapelle-expiatoire.name: Expiatory Chapel
chapelle-expiatoire.description: Neoclassical chapel built between 1815 and 1826 for Louis XVIII on the former Madeleine cemetery, where Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were buried after their execution. Designed by Pierre Fontaine, it is a memorial to victims of the Revolution.

chapelle-foujita.name: Foujita Chapel
chapelle-foujita.description: Notre-Dame-de-la-Paix chapel, built in 1965-1966 to a design by the painter Léonard Foujita, who was baptised in Reims in 1959, and financed by René Lalou, head of the Mumm champagne house. The artist designed its architecture, stained-glass windows and frescoes, and is buried there.

chateau-borely-musee-des-arts-decoratifs.name: Museum of Decorative Arts, Faience and Fashion
chateau-borely-musee-des-arts-decoratifs.description: An 18th-century Marseille bastide built for the Borély family, the château has housed the Museum of Decorative Arts, Faience and Fashion since June 2013. Visitors discover 18th-century furniture and objets d'art, faience from Marseille and Moustiers, Art Nouveau ceramics and fashion pieces.

chateau-d-angers.name: Château d'Angers
chateau-d-angers.description: Fortress built between 1230 and 1242 for Saint Louis and his mother Blanche of Castile, ringed by seventeen towers and more than 800 metres of ramparts overlooking the Maine river. Since 1954 it has housed the Apocalypse Tapestry, woven between 1373 and 1380 for Louis I of Anjou, one of the largest medieval tapestries to survive.

chateau-d-assier.name: Château d'Assier
chateau-d-assier.description: Renaissance château built between 1518 and 1535 by Galiot de Genouillac, master of artillery under François I, on the foundations of a medieval fortress. Largely demolished in the 18th century, only the west wing survives, decorated with a carved frieze celebrating its builder's military exploits.

chateau-d-aulteribe.name: Château d'Aulteribe
chateau-d-aulteribe.description: Stronghold fortified in 1467 by Charles Motier de La Fayette, remodelled in the 19th century in neo-Gothic taste by Joseph de Pierre and his wife Marie-Pauline Onslow. Bequeathed to the state in 1954, the château preserves furniture and tapestries spanning the 15th to 19th centuries.

chateau-d-azay-le-rideau.name: Château d'Azay-le-Rideau
chateau-d-azay-le-rideau.description: Renaissance château built between 1518 and 1527 for Gilles Berthelot, a treasurer to François I, partly raised on piles within the bed of the Indre river. Confiscated by the king after its owner's disgrace, it is today one of the most visited châteaux of the Loire.

chateau-d-if.name: Château d'If
chateau-d-if.description: Fortress built between 1524 and 1531 on the orders of François I to defend Marseille's harbour, converted into a state prison as early as the mid-16th century. Alexandre Dumas imprisoned Edmond Dantès here in The Count of Monte Cristo, making this small rocky island famous worldwide.

chateau-d-oiron.name: Château d'Oiron
chateau-d-oiron.description: Renaissance château of the Gouffier family, notably Claude Gouffier, Grand Squire of France, famed for its 55-metre painted gallery illustrating the Trojan War. State property since 1946, it has hosted the Curios & Mirabilia contemporary art collection, devised by Jean-Hubert Martin, since 1993.

chateau-de-bouges.name: Château de Bouges
chateau-de-bouges.description: Small neoclassical château built in 1765 for Charles Leblanc de Marnaval, in the spirit of the Petit Trianon. Bequeathed in 1967 with its 1,600 pieces of furniture by Henri Viguier, president of the Bazar de l'Hôtel de Ville department store, it is set in an 80-hectare park laid out by Henri and Achille Duchêne.

chateau-de-bussy-rabutin.name: Château de Bussy-Rabutin
chateau-de-bussy-rabutin.description: Fourteenth-century château remodelled during the Renaissance, where the writer Roger de Bussy-Rabutin, exiled by order of Louis XIV after his scandalous Histoire amoureuse des Gaules, spent seventeen years commissioning more than five hundred portraits of the court. His apartments form a satirical gallery of the Sun King's reign.

chateau-de-carrouges.name: Château de Carrouges
chateau-de-carrouges.description: Château of the Blosset and Le Veneur families, built in red and black brick from the 14th century onward and surrounded by moats. Its Louis XII-style gatehouse was commissioned by Cardinal Jean Le Veneur; state property since 1936, it is now managed by the Centre des monuments nationaux.

chateau-de-castelnau-bretenoux.name: Château de Castelnau-Bretenoux
chateau-de-castelnau-bretenoux.description: Red sandstone fortress of the lords of Castelnau, vassals of the counts of Toulouse, built from the 12th century onward on a promontory above the Dordogne valley. Ruined by a fire in 1851, it was restored over thirty years by the opera singer Jean Mouliérat, who bequeathed the château and its collections to the state.

chateau-de-champs-sur-marne.name: Château de Champs-sur-Marne
chateau-de-champs-sur-marne.description: Early 18th-century château east of Paris, once rented by Madame de Pompadour, noted for its rococo interiors, chinoiserie décors and period furniture. Its 85-hectare park combines French formal gardens with landscaped grounds.

chateau-de-chareil-cintrat.name: Château de Chareil-Cintrat
chateau-de-chareil-cintrat.description: Former Bourbon fief remodelled during the Renaissance by Claude Morin, an army administrator who made his fortune during the Italian campaigns. The staircase and a first-floor chamber preserve 16th-century murals depicting the gods of Olympus and an astrological cycle.

chateau-de-chateaudun.name: Château de Châteaudun
chateau-de-chateaudun.description: Fortress founded in 1171, whose 31-metre cylindrical keep, among the oldest in France, dates from 1180. Jean de Dunois, a companion-in-arms of Joan of Arc, had a Gothic residential wing and the Sainte-Chapelle built there between 1452 and 1468; the chapel preserves some fifteen statues of saints.

chateau-de-compiegne-appartements-imperi.name: Château de Compiègne (Imperial Apartments, Museum of the Second Empire, Museum of the Empress, National Carriage Museum)
chateau-de-compiegne-appartements-imperi.description: Palace rebuilt for Louis XV and Louis XVI by Ange-Jacques Gabriel from 1751 onward, later refurnished by Napoleon I and became Napoleon III's favourite residence. It brings together the historic apartments, the Museum of the Second Empire, the Museum of the Empress, and the National Carriage Museum, created in 1927.

chateau-de-coucy.name: Château de Coucy
chateau-de-coucy.description: Fortress built from 1225 by Enguerrand III de Coucy, whose 54-metre cylindrical keep, the tallest in Europe, embodied the lord of Coucy's motto: 'King I am not, nor prince, nor duke, nor count either. I am the lord of Coucy.' It was blown up in 1917 by the retreating German army.

chateau-de-fougeres-sur-bievre.name: Château de Fougères-sur-Bièvre
chateau-de-fougeres-sur-bievre.description: Château rebuilt from 1475 to 1483 for Pierre de Refuge, a treasurer to Louis XI, on the ruins of a fortress destroyed during the Hundred Years' War. A Renaissance gallery with flattened arches was added in the 16th century around the medieval keep, which still stands.

chateau-de-gramont.name: Château de Gramont
chateau-de-gramont.description: Thirteenth-century fortress that passed from Simon de Montfort to the Montaut family, given a Renaissance wing with mullioned windows and a ribbed spiral staircase between 1535 and 1545. Donated to the Centre des monuments nationaux by Monsieur and Madame Dichamp, it retains its original furnishings.

chateau-de-la-motte-tilly.name: Château de la Motte-Tilly
chateau-de-la-motte-tilly.description: Château built from 1754 for the abbé Terray, later controller-general of finances under Louis XV, and kept in the same family until 1972. Entirely refurnished in the 20th century by the Marquise de Maillé, who bequeathed it with its 1,000-hectare estate to the state, on condition that it remain furnished but unlived in.

chateau-de-maisons.name: Château de Maisons
chateau-de-maisons.description: Château built by François Mansart between 1630 and 1646 for René de Longueil, regarded as a founding work of French classical architecture. Its monumental staircase and carved stone interiors influenced the design of Versailles.

chateau-de-montal.name: Château de Montal
chateau-de-montal.description: Renaissance château built between 1519 and 1534 by Jeanne de Balsac d'Entraygues in memory of her son Robert, killed in war in 1523, with an Italian-inspired straight staircase and carved busts of her family. Stripped and sold off in 1880, it was bought back and restored between 1908 and 1913 by the industrialist Maurice Fenaille, who donated it to the state.

chateau-de-pierrefonds.name: Château de Pierrefonds
chateau-de-pierrefonds.description: Fortress begun in 1396 for Louis d'Orléans, dismantled on the orders of Louis XIII in 1617 and left in ruins for two centuries. Napoleon III entrusted its restoration to Eugène Viollet-le-Duc from 1857, who reimagined it as a showcase of medieval architecture.

chateau-de-puyguilhem.name: Château de Puyguilhem
chateau-de-puyguilhem.description: Small Renaissance château built between 1513 and 1535 by Mondot de La Marthonie, first president of the parliament of Guyenne, as a hunting residence inspired by the châteaux of the Loire. Left to decay and then expropriated in 1938, it was restored by the state over some twenty years.

chateau-de-rambouillet.name: Château de Rambouillet
chateau-de-rambouillet.description: Royal then presidential residence set in a vast wooded park, where King François I died in 1547. The visit takes in 18th-century apartments, Marie-Antoinette's dairy and the shell-lined cottage built for the Princess de Lamballe.

chateau-de-sceaux-musee-departemental.name: Château de Sceaux
chateau-de-sceaux-musee-departemental.description: Departmental museum in a 19th-century château at the heart of the estate created for Colbert. Paintings, furniture and Sceaux ceramics evoke the history of the domain and life in Île-de-France, set in a park designed by André Le Nôtre.

chateau-de-talcy.name: Château de Talcy
chateau-de-talcy.description: Château purchased in 1517 by the Florentine banker Bernard Salviati, whose daughter Cassandre, whom Pierre de Ronsard met in 1545, inspired his poem 'Mignonne, allons voir si la rose...'. Catherine de' Medici and Charles IX held a conference between Catholics and Protestants there in 1562.

chateau-de-tours-centre-d-exposition.name: Château de Tours — Exhibition Centre
chateau-de-tours-centre-d-exposition.description: Remains of the former royal fortress on the banks of the Loire, of which the Tour de Guise and the governors' lodge survive. The building is now the exhibition centre of the Tours museums and hosts, in partnership with the Jeu de Paume, exhibitions devoted to photography.

chateau-de-villeneuve-lembron.name: Château de Villeneuve-Lembron
chateau-de-villeneuve-lembron.description: Château built in the late 15th century for Rigaud d'Aureille, chamberlain to Louis XI and then Charles VIII, combining defensive tradition — four round towers and wide moats — with Renaissance comfort. Its rooms preserve lively painted murals, including a caricature portrait of its builder.

chateau-de-vincennes.name: Château de Vincennes
chateau-de-vincennes.description: Medieval royal residence on the eastern edge of Paris, with a 52-metre keep, the tallest of its kind in Europe, and a Sainte-Chapelle begun in 1379. French kings lived here before Versailles; the keep later became a state prison.

chateau-de-voltaire-a-ferney.name: Voltaire's Château at Ferney
chateau-de-voltaire-a-ferney.description: Residence where Voltaire settled in 1758 and lived until his death in 1778, after rebuilding the château and turning the village into a thriving community of 1,500 people through workshops producing watches and silk. Restored between 2015 and 2018, it now displays his apartments and the chapel he built in 1761.

chateau-des-ducs-de-bourbon.name: Château des Ducs de Bourbon
chateau-des-ducs-de-bourbon.description: Former residence of the Dukes of Bourbon, of which the 14th-century keep known as La Mal-Coiffée survives, standing 45 metres high and built by Louis II of Bourbon. Ravaged by fire in 1755 and later converted into a prison, it served as a German military jail from 1940 to 1944 and has been open to visitors since 2007.

chateau-des-ducs-de-bretagne-musee-d-his.name: Château des Ducs de Bretagne — Nantes History Museum
chateau-des-ducs-de-bretagne-musee-d-his.description: Museum opened in 2007 in the buildings of the ducal château, after fifteen years of restoration work. Its thirty-two rooms trace the history of Nantes, from the port city and the Atlantic slave trade to the industries of the 19th and 20th centuries, through several hundred objects.

chateau-des-lumieres-de-luneville.name: Château de Lunéville
chateau-des-lumieres-de-luneville.description: Residence of the Dukes of Lorraine, built from 1703 to 1723 for Leopold I, largely to designs by Germain Boffrand, and nicknamed the "Lorraine Versailles." King Stanislas held his court there and died there in 1766; ravaged by fire in 2003, the château is currently under restoration.

chateau-ducal-de-cadillac.name: Château de Cadillac
chateau-ducal-de-cadillac.description: Château built between 1598 and 1634 for Jean-Louis de Nogaret de La Valette, Duke of Épernon and a favourite of Henri III, in a style already anticipating 17th-century classicism. Painted ceilings, monumental fireplaces and tapestries make up its decor; used as a women's prison from 1822 to 1951, it is now managed by the Centre des monuments nationaux.

chateau-et-remparts-de-la-cite-de-carcas.name: Carcassonne Castle and Ramparts
chateau-et-remparts-de-la-cite-de-carcas.description: Fortified city of Gallo-Roman origin, ringed by a double wall nearly 3 kilometres long with 52 towers, which surrendered to Simon de Montfort during the Albigensian Crusade in 1209. Restored from the 1850s onward by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997.

chateau-musee-de-boulogne-sur-mer-chatea.name: Boulogne-sur-Mer Castle Museum
chateau-musee-de-boulogne-sur-mer-chatea.description: Counts' castle built in the 13th century by Philip Hurepel, standing on the ramparts of the upper town. It has housed the municipal museum since 1988, founded in 1825 and renowned for its collection of Greek vases, its Egyptian antiquities linked to Auguste Mariette, and its Alaskan masks brought back by Alphonse Pinart.

chateau-musee-de-dieppe.name: Dieppe Museum
chateau-musee-de-dieppe.description: A fortified castle begun in 1188 and largely rebuilt in the 15th century, it overlooks the town from the cliffside and has housed the municipal museum since 1923. It holds the largest collection of ivories carved in Dieppe from the 16th to the 20th century, marine paintings, and an extensive collection of prints by Georges Braque.

chateau-musee-de-nemours.name: Nemours Castle Museum
chateau-musee-de-nemours.description: Twelfth-century castle in the centre of Nemours, saved by local artists and opened as a museum in 1903. Its collections centre on fine arts of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including works by sculptor Justin-Chrysostome Sanson.

chateau-royal-de-blois-et-musee-des-beau.name: Château de Blois
chateau-royal-de-blois-et-musee-des-beau.description: Royal residence whose four wings juxtapose four periods: the 13th-century Estates Hall, the brick-and-stone Louis XII wing, the François I wing with its spiral staircase, and the classical wing built for Gaston d'Orléans by François Mansart. The scene of the assassination of the Duke of Guise in 1588, it houses the Museum of Fine Arts.

cite-de-la-dentelle-et-de-la-mode.name: International City of Lace and Fashion, Calais
cite-de-la-dentelle-et-de-la-mode.description: Museum opened in 2009 in the former Boulart lace factory, a brick building from 1874 given a glass façade by architects Alain Moatti and Henri Rivière. It operates working Leavers looms and traces the industrial story of Calais, the world capital of lace, through to its uses in fashion.

cite-des-couteliers.name: City of Cutlers
cite-des-couteliers.description: Showcase of contemporary cutlery-making in Thiers, opened on rue Conchette at the initiative of the town, the French Cutlery Federation and local craftsmen. It presents the products and technical know-how of an industry established in Thiers for seven centuries.

cite-du-vitrail.name: City of Stained Glass
cite-du-vitrail.description: Interpretation centre opened in December 2022 in the Hôtel-Dieu-le-Comte, across 3,000 square metres. Its permanent trail presents, over four levels, stained glass from the 12th to the 21st century and its manufacturing techniques, echoing the glassmaking heritage of the Aube, the richest in France.

cite-internationale-de-la-langue-francai.name: International City of the French Language at the Château de Villers-Cotterêts
cite-internationale-de-la-langue-francai.description: A Renaissance château built by François I from 1532, where the 1539 ordinance mandating French in the kingdom's administrative and judicial acts was signed. Restored and converted into the Cité internationale de la langue française, it reopened in 2023 with a permanent exhibition on the history of French and the Francophone world.

cloitre-de-la-cathedrale-de-bayonne.name: Cloister of Bayonne Cathedral
cloitre-de-la-cathedrale-de-bayonne.description: A 14th-century Gothic rayonnant cloister adjoining the south side of Bayonne's Sainte-Marie Cathedral, one of the largest in France. Its galleries hold tomb recesses and funerary slabs from the 14th to 18th centuries and once served as a meeting place for guilds and neighbourhood assemblies.

cloitre-de-la-cathedrale-de-frejus.name: Cloister of Fréjus Cathedral
cloitre-de-la-cathedrale-de-frejus.description: A two-tiered Romanesque cloister of the 12th century beside Fréjus's Saint-Léonce Cathedral, its upper gallery carried on slender 13th-century Corinthian columns. Its ceiling preserves more than three hundred wooden panels painted in the 14th and 15th centuries with figures, animals and fantastical creatures.

cloitre-de-la-psalette.name: Cloister of the Psalette in Tours
cloitre-de-la-psalette.description: The chapter cloister of Tours Cathedral (Saint-Gatien), its oldest gallery dating from 1442 and combining Gothic and Renaissance work. It housed the psalette, the canons' choir school and scriptorium, and its northeast corner holds a carved spiral staircase reminiscent of the one at the Château de Blois.

cloitre-saint-andre-le-bas.name: Cloister Museum of Saint-André-le-Bas, Vienne
cloitre-saint-andre-le-bas.description: Cloister of the urban abbey of Saint-André-le-Bas, built in the second half of the 12th century and the only surviving remnant of the conventual buildings. Modest in size and regular in plan, it houses a lapidary museum of Christian inscriptions and sculpture from Vienne.

collections-de-la-fondation-de-coubertin.name: Collections of the Coubertin Foundation
collections-de-la-fondation-de-coubertin.description: Museum of the Coubertin Foundation in the Chevreuse valley, devoted to sculpture around the figure of Joseph Bernard and to fine craftsmanship. Bronzes are displayed outdoors in the Jardin des Bronzes, beside the estate's renowned workshops.

colonne-de-la-grande-armee-a-wimille.name: Grande Armée Column at Wimille
colonne-de-la-grande-armee-a-wimille.description: A 54-metre neoclassical column raised at Wimille between 1804 and 1841, funded by the soldiers of the Grande Armée whom Napoleon had gathered at the Camp de Boulogne for a planned invasion of England. Construction stalled after the Empire's fall and resumed under the July Monarchy; the column is topped by a statue of Napoleon.

conciergerie.name: Conciergerie
conciergerie.description: Surviving part of the medieval royal palace on the Île de la Cité, later the Revolution's most notorious prison, where Marie-Antoinette was held before her execution. The Gothic Hall of the Men-at-Arms dates from the early 14th century.

couriot-musee-de-la-mine-puits-couriot.name: Couriot — Mining Museum
couriot-musee-de-la-mine-puits-couriot.description: Former Couriot mine shaft, the main extraction site of the Loire coal basin, worked from 1913 until its closure in 1973 and overlooked by its slag heaps. Turned into a museum in 1991, it preserves the pit-workers' changing room, the lamp room and the winding machinery, and offers visits to a reconstructed gallery.

crypte-archeologique-notre-dame-du-bourg.name: Archaeological Crypt of Notre-Dame-du-Bourg
crypte-archeologique-notre-dame-du-bourg.description: Crypt laid out beneath Notre-Dame-du-Bourg cathedral and opened to the public in 2010, following excavations carried out from 1987 to 1993 by Gabrielle Démians d'Archimbaud. It reveals two millennia of occupation, from the Roman walls of Dinia to the earliest Christian churches, including a polychrome mosaic from the 5th century.

crypte-et-tour-de-la-cathedrale-de-bourg.name: Crypt and Tower of Bourges Cathedral
crypte-et-tour-de-la-cathedrale-de-bourg.description: Beneath the choir of Bourges Cathedral, the lower church and its Romanesque crypt, built between 1195 and 1206 to offset the slope of the ground, hold the kneeling effigies of the Duke and Duchess of Berry. The north tower, rebuilt between 1508 and 1542 after its 1506 collapse, rises 65 metres above the cathedral, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1992.

domaine-de-vizille-musee-de-la-revolutio.name: Domaine de Vizille — Museum of the French Revolution
domaine-de-vizille-musee-de-la-revolutio.description: Château built in the early 17th century for François de Bonne, Duke of Lesdiguières and Constable of France, at the foot of the Belledonne massif. In 1788 it was the setting for the Assembly of Vizille, a prelude to the Estates-General, and has housed the Museum of the French Revolution since 1983, set within extensive grounds.

domaine-national-de-saint-cloud.name: National Estate of Saint-Cloud
domaine-national-de-saint-cloud.description: A former royal and imperial château above the Seine, given by Louis XIV to his brother Philippe d'Orléans in 1658 and laid out with gardens by Le Nôtre; Napoleon I was proclaimed emperor there in 1804. Burned by a shell during the 1870 siege of Paris and later razed, the château itself is gone, but its 460-hectare park, with the Grande Cascade and formal gardens, survives as a national estate.

domaine-national-du-palais-royal.name: Palais-Royal
domaine-national-du-palais-royal.description: A palace built from 1628 by Cardinal Richelieu, who bequeathed it to Louis XIII in 1636; Anne of Austria and the young Louis XIV lived there during the Fronde. Passed to the House of Orléans in 1692, it gained Victor Louis's arcaded galleries in the 1780s, once a fashionable hub of Parisian life, and its garden has held Daniel Buren's striped columns since 1986.

dordonha-pole-patrimonial-et-culturel-in.name: Dordonha, Heritage and Cultural Hub (incl. Costi Museum)
dordonha-pole-patrimonial-et-culturel-in.description: Heritage hub housed in the Petite Mission, an ashlar-stone building from the 1680s extended with 19th-century annexes and listed on the register of historic monuments. It brings together an interpretation centre for the architecture and heritage of Bergerac and the Dordogne, the Costi Museum, and temporary exhibitions.

ecole-musee-de-boulogne-sur-mer.name: The School-Museum of Boulogne-sur-Mer
ecole-musee-de-boulogne-sur-mer.description: Museum of school heritage housed in the former Madame-de-Sévigné nursery school, rebuilt in 1956 by the architect Jean Grosbois on the site of the Saint-Nicolas asylum. Its glass-and-concrete building, designed to give children bright, light-filled spaces, provides the setting for collections devoted to the history of schooling.

ecomusee-94260.name: Grand-Orly Seine Bièvre Ecomuseum
ecomusee-94260.description: Community museum founded in 1979 in the former Cottinville farm in Fresnes, documenting everyday life and social change in the southern suburbs of Paris. It collects residents' objects and memories and presents society-focused exhibitions.

ecomusee-du-pays-de-rennes-la-bintinais.name: Bintinais Ecomuseum
ecomusee-du-pays-de-rennes-la-bintinais.description: Ecomuseum opened in 1987 on the Bintinais farm, a former 62-hectare estate south of Rennes. Its exhibition traces the evolution of the Rennes region since the 12th century through agriculture and rural life; the estate maintains nineteen local animal breeds and orchards of heirloom varieties.

eglise-des-cordeliers-palais-des-ducs-de.name: Palace of the Dukes of Lorraine – Lorraine Museum
eglise-des-cordeliers-palais-des-ducs-de.description: Museum created in 1850 by the Société d'Archéologie Lorraine, spread across the ducal palace and its garden, the Cordeliers complex and the Palais du Gouvernement, all listed as historic monuments. Its 155,000 works trace the history of Lorraine from prehistory to the present day; the ducal palace is under renovation, with the Church of the Cordeliers remaining open.

ensemble-cathedral-du-puy-en-velay.name: Le Puy Cathedral Complex
ensemble-cathedral-du-puy-en-velay.description: A Romanesque cathedral of the 11th–13th centuries built of polychrome volcanic stone on a Byzantine-inspired plan, the historic starting point of the Via Podiensis pilgrim route to Compostela and a place of pilgrimage to its Black Virgin since the Middle Ages. The complex includes a 12th-century Romanesque cloister with carved capitals and a freestanding 56-metre bell tower; it has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1998.

enserune-oppidum-et-musee-archeologique.name: Ensérune Oppidum and Archaeological Museum
enserune-oppidum-et-musee-archeologique.description: Gaulish hilltop settlement continuously occupied from the 6th century BC to the 1st century AD, on a hill between Béziers and Narbonne, one of the most important pre-Roman sites in southern France. Rediscovered in the 19th century and excavated since the early 20th, it yielded a necropolis of nearly 500 graves; the museum displays Greek and Iberian vases along with Celtic weapons found on site.

espace-des-sciences-les-champs-libres.name: Espace des Sciences — Les Champs Libres
espace-des-sciences-les-champs-libres.description: Science centre created in 1984 and housed since 2006 at Les Champs Libres, the Rennes cultural complex designed by Christian de Portzamparc. It combines permanent and temporary exhibitions, Merlin's Laboratory dedicated to hands-on experimentation, and a planetarium with a fourteen-metre hemispherical screen.

espace-dominique-bagouet.name: Espace Dominique Bagouet
espace-dominique-bagouet.description: Municipal exhibition space opened on the esplanade Charles-de-Gaulle in Montpellier, named after the choreographer Dominique Bagouet (1951-1992), founder of the city's national choreographic centre. Its programme brings together regional artists, projects blending art and science, illustration and comic art.

eureka-centre-de-culture-scientifique.name: Eurêka, Science Centre
eureka-centre-de-culture-scientifique.description: Science centre of the city of Chambéry, housed on rue de la République in the Jean-Jacques-Rousseau media library building. Formerly known as Galerie Eurêka, it offers interactive exhibitions and workshops devoted to astronomy, natural science and mountain life.

europa-experience.name: Europa Experience
europa-experience.description: Visitor centre of the European Parliament on Place de la Madeleine, opened in 2022. Interactive displays, a 360-degree cinema and role-play games explain how the European Union works and what it does in daily life.

fondation-arp.name: Arp Foundation
fondation-arp.description: House and studios of artists Jean Arp and Sophie Taeuber-Arp in Clamart, built in 1929 to Taeuber-Arp's own design. Rooms and garden display the couple's sculptures, reliefs and works on paper, kept close to their original arrangement.

fondation-du-doute.name: The Fondation du Doute
fondation-du-doute.description: Museum of contemporary art devoted to the Fluxus movement, born of a project by the artist Ben Vautier on the site of the former Minimes convent, whose first stone was laid in 1619. It presents more than four hundred works and documents by some forty international artists, along with the Wall of Words created by Ben in 1995.

fort-carre.name: Fort Carré
fort-carre.description: Square-plan bastioned fortress built from the 1550s under Henri II, on the Saint-Roch peninsula, around the Tour Saint-Laurent, which rises twenty-six metres above the sea. Vauban inspected it in 1679 and 1682; decommissioned and later restored, it has been open to visitors since 1998.

fort-saint-andre-a-villeneuve-lez-avigno.name: Fort Saint-André
fort-saint-andre-a-villeneuve-lez-avigno.description: Fortress built on Mont Andaon under King Jean II the Good and completed under Charles V by architect Jean de Loubières, who also built the Palais des Papes in Avignon, to assert French royal power across the Rhône from papal Avignon. Its 750-metre wall, twin-towered gatehouse and Tour des Masques still dominate Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, alongside the neighbouring Benedictine abbey.

forteresse-de-salses.name: Fortress of Salses
forteresse-de-salses.description: Fortress built between 1497 and 1503 by the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile to seal the passage between Languedoc and Roussillon on the frontier of the kingdom of France. Semi-buried, with walls 6 to 10 metres thick and four corner towers, it marks the transition from medieval military architecture to flat-trajectory artillery fire; captured by French troops in 1639, it lost its strategic role after the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees.

forum-antique-de-bavay-musee-archeologiq.name: Ancient Forum of Bavay, Archaeological Museum of the Département du Nord
forum-antique-de-bavay-musee-archeologiq.description: Remains of the forum of Bagacum, capital of the Nervii founded under Augustus: more than two and a half hectares of squares, a temple and cryptoporticoes, built between the 1st and late 2nd century. Uncovered after the bombing of 1940, the site is paired with a museum that holds a hoard of three hundred and seventy Roman bronzes.

forum-departemental-des-sciences.name: Villeneuve-d'Ascq Departmental Science Forum
forum-departemental-des-sciences.description: Centre for scientific, technical and industrial culture, opened on 14 December 1996 at the centre François-Mitterrand in Villeneuve-d'Ascq, in a building by the architect Jean-Claude Burdèse. It designs its own interactive exhibitions, hosts touring exhibitions and has a planetarium.

frac-grand-large-hauts-de-france.name: Frac Grand Large — Hauts-de-France
frac-grand-large-hauts-de-france.description: Regional collection of contemporary art for Nord-Pas-de-Calais, created in 1982, transferred to Dunkerque in 1996 and then, in November 2013, into a building by Lacaton & Vassal that exactly duplicates the AP2 hall of the former shipyards. Its collection comprises around 1,500 works of contemporary art and design since the 1960s.

frac-nouvelle-aquitaine-meca.name: Frac Nouvelle-Aquitaine MÉCA
frac-nouvelle-aquitaine-meca.description: Regional collection of contemporary art created in 1982, with more than 1,600 works in which photography holds an important place. Since 2019 it has occupied the MÉCA, a loop-shaped building designed by the architect Bjarke Ingels on the banks of the Garonne, which it shares with ALCA and OARA.

frac-sud-cite-de-l-art-contemporain.name: Frac Sud – Cité de l'Art Contemporain
frac-sud-cite-de-l-art-contemporain.description: Regional collection of contemporary art for Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, created in 1982 and housed since 2013 in a building by the Japanese architect Kengo Kuma, boulevard de Dunkerque, in Marseille's Joliette district. Renamed Frac Sud, it presents its collection along with a collection of artists' books and multiples.

galerie-david-d-angers.name: Galerie David d'Angers
galerie-david-d-angers.description: Museum opened in May 1984 in the former Toussaint abbey church, founded in the 12th century and fitted for the occasion with an overhead glass roof by the architect Pierre Prunet. It brings together nearly seven hundred works by the Angevin sculptor Pierre-Jean David d'Angers (1788-1856), mostly original plaster casts: statues, busts and medallions.

galerie-des-musees-palais-de-l-europe.name: Galerie des Musées (Palais de l'Europe)
galerie-des-musees-palais-de-l-europe.description: Exhibition hall of the Menton museums, set up in the Palais de l'Europe, a former municipal casino inaugurated in 1909 to designs by the Danish architect Hans-Georg Tersling. It hosts rotating hangs, notably around the Jean Cocteau – Séverin Wunderman collection and modern art.

galerie-lapidaire-du-cloitre-saint-corne.name: Lapidary Gallery of the Saint-Corneille Cloister
galerie-lapidaire-du-cloitre-saint-corne.description: The only surviving remnant of the royal abbey of Saint-Corneille, founded in 876 by Charles the Bald and where Hugh Capet was recognised as king in 987: the 14th-century Gothic cloister, spared by the demolitions begun in 1806. It displays sculptures and lapidary fragments from the abbey and from monuments across Compiègne.

galerie-le-chateau-d-eau.name: Le Château d'Eau
galerie-le-chateau-d-eau.description: Brick water tower built from 1821 to 1825 to supply Toulouse, decommissioned and then transformed in 1974 by the photographer Jean Dieuzaide into France's first public gallery devoted to photography. It presents exhibitions and a photographic collection built up since its founding.

granet-xxe-collection-jean-planque-chape.name: Granet XXe – Jean Planque Collection (Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs)
granet-xxe-collection-jean-planque-chape.description: Annexe of the Musée Granet, opened in 2013 in the Carmelite chapel of the White Penitents in Aix-en-Provence. It presents the collection assembled by the Swiss painter and dealer Jean Planque (1910-1998), an adviser to the gallerist Ernst Beyeler, placed on deposit by his foundation: Cézanne, Monet, Picasso and Dubuffet.

grotte-de-pair-non-pair.name: Pair-non-Pair Cave
grotte-de-pair-non-pair.description: Painted cave discovered in 1881 by the self-taught local scholar François Daleau, who excavated over 15,000 flint, bone and ivory tools there until 1887. Its engravings, dated to the Aurignacian period between 37,000 and 32,000 years ago and including a giant deer and a 2.5-metre horse, are among the oldest known and helped establish the authenticity of prehistoric art.

horreum-romain.name: Roman Horreum
horreum-romain.description: Vaulted underground galleries dug in the second half of the 1st century BCE, the only Roman monument still visible in Narbonne. Across some 200 square metres, a central corridor serves small rooms whose function — warehouse, covered market or crawl space — remains debated; the whole complex is listed as a historic monument.

hotel-cabu-musee-d-histoire-et-d-archeol.name: Historical and Archaeological Museum of the Orléanais
hotel-cabu-musee-d-histoire-et-d-archeol.description: Founded in 1823 by the Comte de Bizemont-Prunelé, the museum has occupied the Hôtel Cabu since 1862, a Renaissance mansion known as the house of Diane de Poitiers. It preserves the Neuvy-en-Sullias hoard, an exceptional group of Gallic and Gallo-Roman bronzes, medieval sculpture, and mementos of the Loire and of Joan of Arc.

hotel-de-cabrieres-sabatier-d-espeyran-d.name: Hôtel de Cabrières-Sabatier d'Espeyran (Decorative Arts Department of the Musée Fabre)
hotel-de-cabrieres-sabatier-d-espeyran-d.description: A mansion built in 1874 and bequeathed to the Musée Fabre in 1967 along with its furniture and decor. Now the museum's decorative arts department, it offers a rare record of the lifestyle of the Montpellier bourgeoisie in the second half of the 19th century.

hotel-de-la-marine.name: Hôtel de la Marine
hotel-de-la-marine.description: Ange-Jacques Gabriel's 18th-century palace on Place de la Concorde housed the royal furniture storehouse, then the Navy Ministry for two centuries. Reopened in 2021, it displays restored period apartments and grand salons overlooking the square.

hotel-de-sade.name: Hôtel de Sade
hotel-de-sade.description: Mansion built in 1513 by Balthazar de Sade, an ancestor of the Marquis de Sade, combining flamboyant Gothic and Renaissance styles in the centre of Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Acquired by the state in 1929, it has housed the archaeological museum since 1954, displaying finds from the nearby Roman site of Glanum alongside remains of 4th-century Roman baths and a 16th-century chapel.

hotel-de-sully.name: Hôtel de Sully
hotel-de-sully.description: Mansion built between 1625 and 1630 in the Marais by architect Jean Androuet du Cerceau for the financier Mesme Gallet, then bought in 1634 by Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, who had its interior decorated. Its courtyard and garden façades, adorned with allegorical reliefs of the Seasons and Elements, rank among the finest examples of Louis XIII style; restored, it has housed the headquarters of the Centre des monuments nationaux since 1967.

hotel-dubocage-de-bleville.name: Hôtel Dubocage de Bléville
hotel-dubocage-de-bleville.description: A merchant's house from the 16th and 17th centuries, one of the oldest in Le Havre, whose façade combines black flint, brick and Caen stone. It bears the name of the Le Havre navigator and shipowner Michel Joseph Dubocage de Bléville; listed as a historic monument in 1946, it houses a museum of maritime and merchant history.

institut-d-art-contemporain-iac.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Villeurbanne
institut-d-art-contemporain-iac.description: Institute born in 1998 from the merger of the Nouveau Musée, created in 1978 by Jean-Louis Maubant, and the Rhône-Alpes regional collection of contemporary art. Both an art centre and a public collection, it holds nearly 1,750 works — by Alighiero Boetti, Daniel Buren, Yona Friedman — circulated throughout the region.

jardin-botanique-de-bordeaux-site-de-la-.name: Bordeaux Botanical Garden (Bastide Site)
jardin-botanique-de-bordeaux-site-de-la-.description: An extension of the botanical garden founded in 1629, this contemporary site laid out on the right bank of the Garonne was designed by the landscape architect Catherine Mosbach and the architect Françoise-Hélène Jourda. Over six hundred metres it unfolds a field of forty-four cultivated plots, a gallery of habitats evoking eleven Aquitaine landscapes, a water garden and greenhouses.

jardins-du-musee-international-de-la-par.name: Gardens of the International Perfume Museum (JMIP)
jardins-du-musee-international-de-la-par.description: A 2.7-hectare garden opened in 2013 in Mouans-Sartoux, an offshoot of the International Perfume Museum in Grasse. More than seven hundred plant species are cultivated there, including the perfume plants of the Grasse region — May rose, jasmine, tuberose; the site has held the Jardin Remarquable label since 2022.

l-aubette-1928.name: L'Aubette 1928
l-aubette-1928.description: A classical building on place Kléber, built from 1765 to 1778 by Jacques-François Blondel, whose right wing was transformed in 1926-1928 into a leisure complex by Theo van Doesburg, Sophie Taeuber-Arp and Hans Arp. Covered over as early as 1938 and rediscovered in the 1970s, these abstract decors have been restored and are visible once again.

l-ensemble-de-l-uvre-de-la-misericorde.name: The Œuvre de la Miséricorde Complex
l-ensemble-de-l-uvre-de-la-misericorde.description: Charitable institution founded in 1622 by the Ladies of the Miséricorde, established in 1715 in a house bequeathed by Anne-Madeleine de Conty d'Argencourt and equipped with an apothecary opened in 1718. Listed as a historic monument in 2003, the complex displays some four hundred objects tracing the hospital and pharmaceutical history of Montpellier.

la-cinematheque-francaise.name: La Cinémathèque française
la-cinematheque-francaise.description: Film archive and museum founded in 1936 by Henri Langlois, housed in a Frank Gehry building in Bercy. Its Musée Méliès traces cinema history through cameras, costumes and magic-lantern devices, alongside daily screenings and exhibitions.

la-crypte-de-boulogne-sur-mer.name: The Crypt of Boulogne-sur-Mer
la-crypte-de-boulogne-sur-mer.description: A vast underground network laid out in the 19th century beneath the Basilica of Notre-Dame, layering Roman remains, a Romanesque crypt and galleries entirely covered with frescoes. Around one hundred and fifty pieces of sacred art are displayed there, including the reliquary of the Holy Blood given by Philip the Fair in 1308.

la-fabrique-des-savoirs.name: Fabrique des Savoirs
la-fabrique-des-savoirs.description: Museum and archive centre opened in 2010 in part of the former Blin & Blin cloth mill, a witness to Elbeuf's woollen-textile past. Awarded the Musée de France label, it holds some 45,000 objects: textile machinery, archaeological pieces, taxidermy specimens, paintings and antique fabrics.

la-kunsthalle-mulhouse.name: La Kunsthalle Mulhouse
la-kunsthalle-mulhouse.description: Contemporary art centre of the city of Mulhouse, housed on the second floor of La Fonderie, the former assembly hall of the Société Alsacienne de Constructions Mécaniques, converted into a university campus in 2007. With no permanent collection, it produces exhibitions and hosts artists in residence; it has held the label of contemporary art centre of national interest since 2019.

la-maison-elysee.name: La Maison Élysée
la-maison-elysee.description: Visitor space opposite the Élysée Palace at 88 rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré, combining a small museum, boutique and tea room. Objects, portraits and a 3D film retrace the palace's history from the 1722 Hôtel d'Évreux to the present-day presidency.

la-manufacture-musee-de-la-memoire-et-de.name: La Manufacture, Museum of Textile Memory and Creation
la-manufacture-musee-de-la-memoire-et-de.description: Museum housed in the workshops of the former textile firm Craye et Fils, opened in 2001 under the name Musée du Jacquard, then renovated and reopened in 2015. Visitors can see working looms, from medieval models to computer-assisted machines, alongside testimony from textile workers.

la-piscine-musee-d-art-et-d-industrie-an.name: La Piscine, Museum of Art and Industry
la-piscine-musee-d-art-et-d-industrie-an.description: Former Art Deco municipal swimming pool, built from 1927 to 1932 by the architect Albert Baert around a fifty-metre pool, converted into a museum by Jean-Paul Philippon and inaugurated in 2001. It brings together 19th- and 20th-century fine arts, textiles, fashion and ceramics, with works by Camille Claudel and Tamara de Lempicka.

laac-lieu-d-art-et-action-contemporaine.name: LAAC — Centre for Contemporary Art and Action, Dunkerque
laac-lieu-d-art-et-action-contemporaine.description: Museum of contemporary art born from the association founded in 1974 by the engineer Gilbert Delaine and inaugurated in 1982 in a building by Jean Willerval, surrounded by a sculpture garden. Its roughly 1,500 works span creation from 1945 to 1980, from CoBrA to Lyrical Abstraction and the Nouveaux Réalistes, including the northern French artists Eugène Leroy and Eugène Dodeigne.

labanque-centre-de-production-et-de-diff.name: Labanque — Centre for the Production and Dissemination of Visual Arts
labanque-centre-de-production-et-de-diff.description: Art centre set up in the former Béthune branch of the Banque de France, built in 1912 by the architect Defrasse and extended from 1924 to 1927, with a regionalist façade of red brick and ashlar stone. Opened in 2007 and reopened in 2016 after renovation, it spreads 1,500 square metres of exhibition space over four levels.

lam-lille-metropole-musee-d-art-moderne-.name: LaM — Lille Métropole Museum of Modern Art, Contemporary Art and Art Brut
lam-lille-metropole-musee-d-art-moderne-.description: Museum born from the 1979 donation of the Roger Dutilleul and Jean Masurel collection, opened in 1983 in a building by Roland Simounet set within a sculpture park. Extended in 2010 by Manuelle Gautrand for the L'Aracine collection, it brings together modern art (Picasso, Braque, Léger, Modigliani) and the largest public collection of art brut in France.

le-carmel.name: Le Carmel
le-carmel.description: Former Carmelite monastery founded in 1870 by nuns from Bagnères-de-Bigorre, occupied until the community's departure in 1988 and bought by the city of Tarbes in 1994. Its chapel, converted into a 200-square-metre exhibition hall, hosts modern and contemporary art.

le-chronographe.name: Le Chronographe
le-chronographe.description: Archaeological interpretation centre opened in January 2017 in Rezé, in a building by Jérôme Berranger and Stéphanie Vincent erected on the edge of the excavation site. It introduces visitors to Ratiatum, a Gallo-Roman port on the Loire active from the 1st to the 3rd century, and its links with the Roman Empire.

le-donjon-de-niort.name: Niort Keep
le-donjon-de-niort.description: Romanesque keep built in the late 12th century by the Plantagenets, Henry II and then Richard the Lionheart, on the banks of the Sèvre Niortaise. Formed of two square towers linked by a 15th-century residential range, it served as a prison before being opened to visitors and hosting exhibitions.

le-feru-des-sciences-ancien-musee-de-l-h.name: Le Féru des Sciences (former Museum of the History of Iron)
le-feru-des-sciences-ancien-musee-de-l-h.description: Museum inaugurated on 14 October 1966 in a modernist glass-and-steel building designed by Jacques and Michel André with Claude Prouvé, formed of two wings linked by a gallery. Renamed Féru des Sciences in 2022, it holds more than 13,000 objects tracing the history of iron and the steel industry.

le-magasin-centre-national-d-art-contemp.name: Magasin — National Centre for Contemporary Art
le-magasin-centre-national-d-art-contemp.description: Contemporary art centre housed in a metal hall built by the Eiffel workshops for the 1900 Universal Exposition, then re-erected in Grenoble by the industrialist Hippolyte Bouchayer. Restored by the architect Patrick Bouchain, it has hosted temporary exhibitions since 1986, often produced on site with the artists, on the model of the German Kunsthallen.

le-plateau-frac-ile-de-france.name: Le Plateau – Frac Île-de-France
le-plateau-frac-ile-de-france.description: Exhibition space of the Fonds régional d'art contemporain d'Île-de-France, in the Buttes-Chaumont district of the 19th arrondissement. It presents several contemporary art shows a year, drawing on the regional collection and emerging or international artists.

le-quadrilatere.name: Le Quadrilatère
le-quadrilatere.description: Building constructed in 1976 by the architect André Hermant to house the National Tapestry Gallery, at the foot of Beauvais Cathedral. It stands on the Gallo-Roman rampart, whose remains can be visited in the basement, and today combines contemporary art exhibitions with a heritage interpretation centre.

le-rize.name: Le Rize
le-rize.description: Municipal facility in Villeurbanne bringing together the city archives, a media library and exhibition rooms around the motto "memories, cultures, exchanges." Each season, through exhibitions, talks and research projects, it explores the social history and collective memory of the town's residents.

le-signe-centre-national-du-graphisme.name: Le Signe — National Graphic Design Centre
le-signe-centre-national-du-graphisme.description: Art centre dedicated to graphic design, inaugurated on 6 October 2016 in the former Banque de France building, redesigned by the Moatti-Rivière agency. It continues a tradition born from the bequest of 5,000 illustrated posters made to Chaumont by Gustave Dutailly in 1905, and later from the international poster festival, and holds some 40,000 contemporary posters.

les-abattoirs-musee-frac-occitanie-toulo.name: Les Abattoirs
les-abattoirs-musee-frac-occitanie-toulo.description: Former brick slaughterhouses built from 1827 to 1831 by the architect Urbain Vitry around a large central scalding hall, listed in 1990 and converted into a museum opened in 2000. They bring together Toulouse's collections of modern and contemporary art and the Frac Occitanie, and preserve the stage curtain painted by Picasso and Luis Fernández in 1936.

les-arenes-de-saintes-amphitheatre-gallo.name: The Arena of Saintes (Gallo-Roman Amphitheatre)
les-arenes-de-saintes-amphitheatre-gallo.description: Amphitheatre of Mediolanum Santonum, begun under Augustus and completed under Claudius, one of the oldest in Gaul, set against the slopes of a natural valley. Measuring 126 by 102 metres, it could hold some fifteen thousand spectators; abandoned in the 4th century and later quarried for stone, it has been listed as a historic monument since 1840.

les-bains-pommer.name: Pommer Baths
les-bains-pommer.description: Public bathhouse created in 1891 by Auguste Pommer, which combined, across more than 500 square metres, public bathrooms, twelve rental apartments and a garden. In operation until 1972 and listed as a historic monument in 1992, it is today a municipal museum of Avignon.

les-charmettes-maison-de-jean-jacques-ro.name: Les Charmettes — Jean-Jacques Rousseau's House
les-charmettes-maison-de-jean-jacques-ro.description: An 18th-century country house nestled in a valley south of Chambéry, where Jean-Jacques Rousseau stayed with Madame de Warens between 1736 and 1742. A place of literary pilgrimage from as early as the late 18th century, it preserves its period decor, the philosopher's bedroom, and a garden of vines and fruit trees opening onto the mountains.

les-pecheries-musee-de-fecamp.name: Les Pêcheries — Fécamp Museum
les-pecheries-musee-de-fecamp.description: Opened in December 2017 on the harbour, in a former 1950 cod-drying plant restored by the Basalt Architecture agency. It brings together Fécamp's municipal collections, previously divided between the Museum of Newfoundland Fishermen and Fishing and the Museum of Art and Childhood, and ends in a belvedere looking out over the English Channel.

lugdunum-musee-et-theatres-romains.name: Lugdunum — Museum and Roman Theatres
lugdunum-musee-et-theatres-romains.description: Gallo-Roman museum set into the hillside of Fourvière, inaugurated in 1975 to designs by Bernard Zehrfuss, its concrete ramps spiralling downward and opening through wide bays onto the ancient theatre and odeon of Lugdunum. Its collections bring together the Claudian Tablet, the Coligny calendar, a bronze Neptune, and a remarkable collection of mosaics.

madd-bordeaux-musee-des-arts-decoratifs-.name: Bordeaux Museum of Decorative Arts
madd-bordeaux-musee-des-arts-decoratifs-.description: The museum occupies the Hôtel de Lalande, a mansion built in 1778 for a councillor of the Parlement of Bordeaux. Created in 1924, it displays 18th- and 19th-century furniture and wood panelling, silverware, and Bordeaux porcelain and faience, and broadened its scope to contemporary design in 2013.

mahb-musee-d-art-et-d-histoire-baron-ger.name: Baron-Gérard Museum
mahb-musee-d-art-et-d-histoire-baron-ger.description: Bayeux's museum of art and history, housed in the former episcopal palace, whose buildings span the 11th to the 16th century. Reopened in 2013 after a long campaign of works, it has borne the name of Baron Gérard since 1951 and brings together archaeology, old master and Impressionist paintings, and above all the porcelain and lace that made the city's reputation.

maison-alexandra-david-neel.name: Alexandra David-Néel's House
maison-alexandra-david-neel.description: Villa that the explorer and orientalist Alexandra David-Néel bought in 1928 on her return from Tibet and named Samten Dzong, "fortress of meditation," before extending it with terraces and a tower that give it an Anglo-Tibetan appearance. Bequeathed to the town of Digne-les-Bains on her death in 1969, it preserves her Asian collections, her bedroom and her study.

maison-berges-musee-de-la-houille-blanch.name: Maison Bergès — Museum of White Coal
maison-berges-musee-de-la-houille-blanch.description: Residence of the paper engineer Aristide Bergès, a pioneer of hydroelectric power, at the foot of the Belledonne range. Its Art Nouveau interiors, preserved with their original decor and furnishings, provide the setting for a museum devoted to "white coal" (hydroelectricity) and the industrialisation of the Grésivaudan valley.

maison-d-ernest-renan-a-treguier.name: Ernest Renan's House
maison-d-ernest-renan-a-treguier.description: Half-timbered house in Tréguier where the writer and philosopher Ernest Renan was born in 1823 and lived until he was fifteen. Donated to the state by his granddaughters, it is now a museum displaying period Breton furniture, a reconstruction of his office at the Collège de France, and mementos of his sister Henriette.

maison-de-balzac.name: Balzac's House
maison-de-balzac.description: The writer's modest house in Passy, the only one of Balzac's Paris homes still standing, where he lived from 1840 to 1847 and corrected La Comédie humaine. Manuscripts, portraits and his famous turquoise-studded cane evoke his life and work.

maison-de-george-sand-a-nohant.name: George Sand's House
maison-de-george-sand-a-nohant.description: 18th-century château in the Berry region, inherited by George Sand in 1821 and where she settled permanently in 1853 after hosting Chopin, Liszt, Balzac, Flaubert and Delacroix; she died there in 1876. The house preserves her furniture, natural history collections, and the puppet theatre created by her son Maurice in 1847.

maison-de-georges-clemenceau-a-saint-vin.name: Georges Clemenceau's House
maison-de-georges-clemenceau-a-saint-vin.description: Traditional Vendée farmhouse facing the Atlantic at Saint-Vincent-sur-Jard, where Georges Clemenceau retired after his defeat in the 1920 presidential election and lived until his death in 1929. The museum preserves his furniture and belongings, including Japanese diplomatic gifts, along with an impressionist-style garden inspired by his friend Claude Monet's garden at Giverny.

maison-de-l-armateur.name: Shipowner's House
maison-de-l-armateur.description: Neoclassical mansion built from 1790 onward by the architect Paul-Michel Thibault and acquired in 1800 by the merchant Martin-Pierre Foäche. Its five storeys are arranged around an octagonal light well; a survivor of the 1944 bombing raids, it displays furniture, paintings, maps and nautical instruments evoking the great maritime trade of Le Havre.

maison-de-la-dentelle-ecole-dentelliere.name: Maison de la Dentelle — Lace School
maison-de-la-dentelle-ecole-dentelliere.description: A venue devoted to the bobbin lace of Bailleul, a textile tradition of French Flanders, located on rue du Collège. The lace school keeps this craft alive through classes and demonstrations, and shows the public the finished pieces and tools of the trade.

maison-de-la-magie-robert-houdin.name: Maison de la Magie Robert-Houdin
maison-de-la-magie-robert-houdin.description: Museum of illusion housed in the Hôtel Ballet, built in 1856 opposite the Château de Blois, the birthplace of the illusionist Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin. Opened in 1998, the only public museum in Europe to combine magic collections with permanent shows, it is marked by the dragon heads that emerge from its façade every half hour.

maison-de-la-photographie-ma-p.name: Maison de la Photographie (Ma.P)
maison-de-la-photographie-ma-p.description: Municipal gallery opened in 2002 in Toulon's old town, near place du Globe, where it occupies a former hammam whose circular structure it has retained. Its temporary programme covers photography in all its forms, from humanist reportage to the Provençal school and fine-art photography.

maison-de-victor-hugo.name: Victor Hugo's House
maison-de-victor-hugo.description: The apartment on Place des Vosges where Victor Hugo lived from 1832 to 1848, now a museum. Drawings, manuscripts, portraits and the Chinese-style salon he created for Juliette Drouet retrace the writer's life from childhood to exile.

maison-des-ailleurs.name: La Maison des Ailleurs
maison-des-ailleurs.description: House where the Rimbaud family lived from 1869 to 1875, the years of Arthur Rimbaud's great poems, opened to the public in 2004 for the 150th anniversary of his birth. Through sound and visual installations, each room evokes the poet's elsewheres: Paris, Brussels, London, Java, Aden and Harar.

maison-des-jardies.name: Jardies House
maison-des-jardies.description: A former vintner's house in Sèvres where Balzac lived from 1837 to 1840 and where Léon Gambetta died in 1882. Run by the Centre des monuments nationaux, it keeps Gambetta's rooms as they were, with a Bartholdi monument in the garden.

maison-des-lumieres-denis-diderot.name: Maison des Lumières Denis Diderot
maison-des-lumieres-denis-diderot.description: Museum devoted to the Age of Enlightenment and to Denis Diderot, born in Langres in 1713, housed in the Hôtel du Breuil de Saint-Germain, a mansion dating from the 16th and 18th centuries. Inaugurated on 5 October 2013 for the writer's tercentenary, it spreads across four levels some 250 objects devoted to his youth in Langres, his life in Paris, and the Encyclopédie.

maison-des-musees.name: Maison des Musées
maison-des-musees.description: Reception and outreach space opened by the city of Bourges in the former Museum of the Best Craftsmen of France, during the renovation of its museum venues. It traces two centuries of the history of the municipal collections, complemented by displays of works and an annual themed exhibition upstairs.

maison-mantin.name: Maison Mantin
maison-mantin.description: Eclectic residence built from 1894 to 1897 for Louis Mantin, a man of independent means and collector from Moulins, blending neo-Gothic and neo-Renaissance references and fitted with the most modern comforts: electricity, running water, underfloor heating. Bequeathed to the town on his death in 1905 to be preserved intact, it reopened in 2010 after seventy years of closure.

maison-maurice-viollette.name: Maison Maurice-Viollette
maison-maurice-viollette.description: Dreux's museum of art and history, housed in the home of Maurice Viollette, mayor of the town from 1908 to 1959 and a former governor-general of Algeria. Its collections combine archaeology, medieval stained glass and sculpture from the Collégiale Saint-Étienne, and 19th-century paintings, including a study of wisteria by Claude Monet.

maison-musee-maurice-ravel.name: Maurice Ravel House-Museum
maison-musee-maurice-ravel.description: Le Belvédère, the small house in Montfort-l'Amaury where Maurice Ravel lived from 1921 to 1937 and composed Boléro among other works. Its rooms preserve his furniture, mechanical toys and decor exactly as the composer arranged them.

maison-natale-de-charles-trenet.name: Charles Trenet's Birthplace
maison-natale-de-charles-trenet.description: A house with green shutters on the avenue that now bears his name, where Charles Trenet was born on 18 May 1913 and which he described as "that old shack full of memories." Opened to the public in 2000, it offers an audiovisual, interactive trail combining archival documents and the singer's personal belongings.

maison-natale-de-louis-braille.name: Louis Braille's Birthplace
maison-natale-de-louis-braille.description: The family home in Coupvray where Louis Braille was born in 1809, with the saddlery workshop where he lost his sight as a child. The museum retraces his life and the invention of the raised-dot alphabet used by blind readers worldwide.

maison-natale-de-victor-hugo.name: Victor Hugo's Birthplace
maison-natale-de-victor-hugo.description: First-floor apartment at 140 Grande Rue in Besançon, where Victor Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 while his father was stationed there with his garrison. Bought by the town in 1932 and opened as a museum in 2013, it is devoted to the writer's humanist causes: poverty, the death penalty, freedom of expression and children's rights.

maison-natale-du-marechal-foch.name: Marshal Foch's Birthplace
maison-natale-du-marechal-foch.description: A house from the late Louis XV period, built of river pebbles, where Ferdinand Foch was born in 1851 and spent his first twelve years while his father served as secretary-general of the prefecture. Listed as a historic monument in 1938 and opened as a museum in 1951 for the marshal's centenary, it preserves its furniture and walnut fireplaces.

maison-rouge-musee-des-vallees-cevenoles.name: Museum of the Cévennes Valleys
maison-rouge-musee-des-vallees-cevenoles.description: The museum occupies the Maison Rouge silk mill, France's first industrial silk-spinning mill and the last in the country to close, in 1965. Opened to the public in 2018, it presents the 10,000 objects gathered by Daniel Travier on everyday life, agriculture, livestock farming and crafts in the Cévennes valleys.

mamc-musee-d-art-moderne-et-contemporain.name: Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art of Saint-Étienne Métropole
mamc-musee-d-art-moderne-et-contemporain.description: Opened in 1987 in Saint-Priest-en-Jarez, on the edge of Saint-Étienne, in a building by the architect Didier Guichard clad in black ceramic tiles, echoing the region's industrial architecture. It holds one of the leading French public collections of modern and contemporary art, from the early 20th century to the present day.

manas-musee-d-art-naif-et-des-arts-singu.name: Museum of Naive Art and Art Singulier
manas-musee-d-art-naif-et-des-arts-singu.description: France's first museum devoted to naive art, created in 1967 after the painter Jules Lefranc, a native of Laval, donated his collection.
